Fit a Model

Source: R/statmod.R
statmod.Rd

Fits a distributional regression. One formula carries an equation per parameter of the response distribution, so a scale or a shape is modeled as readily as a mean; the terms that those equations name are assembled into a penalized likelihood and fitted, and any smoothing parameters or prior scales are estimated from the data.

Returns a StatmodFit(), which summary.StatmodFit(), predict.StatmodFit(), coef.StatmodFit() and the other accessors read.

Usage

statmod(
  formula,
  distrib,
  data,
  weights = NULL,
  offsets = NULL,
  inner_optimizer = iwls(),
  inner_information = auto_info(),
  outer_criterion = reml(),
  sparse_criterion = bic(),
  outer_optimizer = NULL,
  start = NULL,
  linpar_control = linpar_options(),
  verbose = 0,
  threads = 1,
  cores = 1,
  ...
)

Arguments

formula

The model formula.

distrib

A distributions7 distribution object.

data

A data frame. Missing values in the response or in a variable that an equation uses are rejected, with the variable and the rows.

weights

Optional prior weights, a numeric vector of length \(n\) or the name of a column of data. The weights must be non-negative, finite and complete, and are taken as given and not normalized. They multiply the log-likelihood, so they act as frequency weights: a constant weight \(c\) on every row is \(c\) copies of the data, and the restricted (REML) criterion counts \(n c\) observations against the coefficients. The REML estimate of a dispersion therefore changes under a constant rescaling of the weights, and the ML estimate does not.

offsets

Optional named list of offsets, one entry per distribution parameter, each of length 1 or \(n\). An offset written in the formula is added to the entry for the same parameter.

inner_optimizer

How the smooth block is fitted: iwls() (the default) or an optimizers7 optimizer. Beside a structural term of the filter shape, the coefficients and the term's parameters are fitted in one system, for which iwls() stands for the system's own default optimizer and an optimizers7 optimizer is used as given.

inner_information

The matrix of second derivatives that the inner fit uses, an object that inherits from distributions7::Information: distributions7::observed_info() (the observed Hessian), distributions7::expected_info() (the Fisher information, whose method is NULL for the closed form of the family or distributions7::expect_opg(), or one of distributions7::expect_opg(), distributions7::expect_integrate() and distributions7::expect_mc(); see distributions7::expected_derivative_methods) or auto_info() (the default), which is settled against the family. With iwls() the matrix is inverted at each step (Newton for the observed information, Fisher scoring for the expected one); with an optimizers7 optimizer it is the Hessian that the optimizer receives, so that inner_optimizer = optimizers7::newton() with inner_information = distributions7::expected_info() takes the expected information. A named matrix is the only one that the inner fit uses. auto_info() chooses the expected information where the family writes it exactly and at an acceptable cost, and the observed information otherwise; with iwls() it also lets the run change matrix and lets the expected information take a step that the observed one cannot (see information_objects). The fitted model records the settled object, and every later refit of the model (the folds of a cross-validation, the restricted fits of a test, the resampled fits of a bootstrap) reads the same one. Beside a score-driven filter (modelterms7::gas()) the coefficients and the filter's own parameters are fitted in one system, whose Hessian is the observed information, or the expected information conditional on the past where distributions7::expected_info() is named here (Fisher scoring over that system); auto_info() leaves that system on the observed information. A model with a term of the likelihood shape (modelterms7::regime(), a marginal break-point term) has no expected information, and distributions7::expected_info() is an error there. The outer criterion has its own information (see reml()) and the standard errors have theirs (see vcov_method); the three choices are independent.

outer_criterion

How the smooth hyperparameters are estimated: reml() (the default), ml(), aic() or bic(), or NULL to hold them where their terms left them. cv() cross-validates the hyperparameter of a kinked penalty only: it is passed as sparse_criterion, and as outer_criterion it is an error. A prediction-error criterion beside a kinked penalty is rejected unless sparse_criterion is NULL.

sparse_criterion

How the hyperparameter of a kinked penalty (lasso, elastic net, scad, mcp) is chosen: bic() (the default), aic(), cv(), or NULL. With NULL the hyperparameter is held at its value, unless the model also carries a smooth penalty and outer_criterion is a prediction-error criterion, which then sweeps the path. A marginal criterion is rejected here, because it is read at a mode that sits on the kink.

outer_optimizer

The optimizer that searches over the smooth hyperparameters, or NULL to choose one from the derivatives of the criterion that exist: optimizers7::newton() where the exact Hessian is usable, optimizers7::lbfgs() with the exact gradient, optimizers7::brent() for one coordinate without a gradient, and optimizers7::nelder_mead() otherwise.

start

Where the fit begins: a named list of coefficients, a start_strategy() such as start_search() or start_from(), which takes the estimates of a model already fitted, or NULL for start_intercepts(). A strategy runs once, before the alternation between the coefficients and the hyperparameters begins. A global search therefore belongs here and not in inner_optimizer, where it would run again at every hyperparameter value that the outer search tries.

linpar_control

How the unpenalized parametric block is built, as linpar_options() returns it: the storage and the contrasts for its factors. It reaches the implicit term, the one into which the bare covariates collapse and which a caller never writes; a modelterms7::linpar() written out takes them directly. The argument and the function are named differently on purpose, as stats::glm()'s control and stats::glm.control() are.

verbose

A level from 0 to 3, or a named logical vector with any of outer, blocks, inner and optimizer.

threads

How many threads the fit may use inside this R process, a single whole number (see numericals7::local_threads()). The default, 1, is sequential and takes the sequential code path. A larger count is passed to the compiled per-observation kernels of the family and to the dense assembly products; below a kernel's internal size threshold the computation stays sequential whatever the count, and a sparse design keeps its Matrix route. Between the default and a count above one the route can change where the work is large (the BLAS crossproduct against the compiled one, and the pivoted qr() against the compiled triangular factor), and the results then agree to rounding. threads counts threads that share memory in one process; the number of separate R processes is cores.

cores

The number of separate R processes, a single whole number (default 1, no process besides this one). The units that are independent by construction are fanned out over them: the folds of a cross-validation, and the combinations of a kinked path's product grid, each of which restarts its warm chain from the sweep's own starting coefficients. Each unit fits sequentially, so threads and cores never nest. The points within one chain stay sequential, because a point fitted from a cold start costs more than one warm-started from the previous point, and splitting a chain would slow the single-process default or make the result depend on the count. For any two values of cores the result is identical bit for bit: the folds are seeded per fold and collected in fold order.

...

Not used. A named argument signals an error. A hyperparameter is held in the term that carries the penalty.

Value

A StatmodFit() object.

The formula

The equations are separated by |, and the first carries the response:

    y ~ x1 + ridge(R) + lasso(L)  |  sigma ~ z  |  nu ~ 1

A parameter with no equation of its own is given an intercept, so y ~ x on a two-parameter family fits a constant scale. statmod_equations() does the split. R's operator precedence nests the equations on the left, so the right-hand side of the whole formula holds only the last equation, and the split walks down the left side instead.

The terms available are modelterms7's: modelterms7::s(), modelterms7::te(), modelterms7::random(), modelterms7::ridge(), modelterms7::lasso(), modelterms7::seg(), modelterms7::nl(), modelterms7::gas() and the rest. Bare covariates collapse into one parametric block. A formula can carry one structural term, which is modelterms7::gas(), modelterms7::regime() or the marginal break-point term, or one modelterms7::gas() term in each of several equations, which are filtered jointly as one recursion.

A structural term whose level adds a constant to the predictor, the \(\omega\) of modelterms7::gas() or the first level of modelterms7::regime(), is confounded with an intercept in the same equation. The intercept is kept and the level held at zero, reported as omega (held) for modelterms7::gas() and as level1 (held) for modelterms7::regime(); writing 0 + gas(...) estimates the level instead. The two spellings are the same model with the same log-likelihood, and the constants differ because they measure different quantities: for a score-driven term the intercept is the stationary level \(\omega / (1 - \sum_j \xi_j)\), which is \(\omega\) divided by one minus the sum of the persistences \(\xi_j\). The page of modelterms7::gas() gives the identity.

The fitting scheme

The terms split in two by a property that each one already reports.

A term whose penalty is twice differentiable in its coefficients, an unpenalized block, a ridge, a spline or a random effect, is estimated in one system by inner_optimizer. Their joint curvature exists, and using it closes a fit in a handful of iterations.

A term whose penalty has a kink, a lasso, an elastic net, a SCAD or an MCP, is estimated as a block of its own while the other blocks are held fixed. The block is fitted by a compiled coordinate descent where the penalty describes its proximal operator as a table at the step taken, and otherwise by an accelerated proximal gradient. Where the equation has a free unpenalized intercept, the descent centers the block and moves that intercept jointly with it.

A structural term of the filter shape, modelterms7::gas(), is fitted in one system with the coefficients. A structural term of the likelihood shape, modelterms7::regime() or the marginal break-point term, is alternated with them.

The fit alternates between the blocks until the relative change of the objective falls below the tolerance. Where a kinked block or a structural term is present, the point reached must in addition satisfy the optimality conditions of the smooth part and of every coefficient held at a kink, and converged reports that reading.

The objective is not averaged

The objective is minus the weighted log-likelihood plus the penalties at full size. A penalty is a negative log-prior, and a posterior adds a log-likelihood and a log-prior at full size; averaging one of them would make a hyperparameter mean something that depends on \(n\). The stopping rule is scaled instead, so a threshold means the same at \(n = 10\) and at \(n = 10^7\).

The weights multiply the log-likelihood, so they act as frequency weights: a constant weight \(c\) on every row is \(c\) copies of the data. The restricted (REML) criterion then counts \(n c\) observations against the \(p\) coefficients, so the REML estimate of a dispersion changes under a constant rescaling of the weights, and the ML estimate does not.

The budget and the stopping rule belong to the method

There is no maxit and no tol here. Both are set on inner_optimizer, which is iwls(maxit =, tol =) or an optimizers7 optimizer with its own maxit and criterion. The alternation reads them from there as its budget in passes and its relative tolerance on the objective, so that one setting governs both the inner fit and the alternation.

Every hyperparameter is estimated unless its term holds it

The term that carries the penalty states which hyperparameters are held: lasso(x, lambda = 3), ridge(x, lambda = 0.5), s(x, bspline_smooth(), hyper = c(lambda = 2)), enet(x, alpha = 0.5). Every hyperparameter left NULL, which is each term's default, is estimated from the data. A hyperparameter is held in the term and nowhere else, so that the model has one statement of each held value.

The smooth hyperparameters go to outer_criterion, reml() by default. outer_optimizer searches over them, and the coefficients are refitted at each point.

A kinked penalty has its own argument. sparse_criterion, bic() by default, sweeps its hyperparameters along a path of their own values, from the kink that empties the block down to a fraction of it. The penalized mode is only piecewise smooth in such a hyperparameter, turning a corner whenever a coefficient joins the active set or leaves it, so a gradient search on a criterion read there would meet those corners.

The top of that path is the kink that empties the block, found at the coefficients in hand and not at a refitted null. It therefore depends on the data and on the rest of the model, since the fits of the other terms enter it.

Where a model carries both kinds, the path is outside and the marginal criterion is estimated inside each of its points, so a smoothing parameter can come from REML and a lasso's \(\lambda\) from BIC in one fit.

With the default marginal = NULL, reml() and ml() also estimate on the criterion the unpenalized coefficients of every distribution parameter other than the first. outer_criterion therefore runs when the model carries a smooth hyperparameter or such a coefficient, and on an ordinary y ~ x with a two-parameter family it estimates the dispersion by REML. Beside a kinked penalty, a structural term or a block that moves with its coefficients, the default names no coefficient, so a model whose only penalties are kinked does not run the criterion. The default criterion is also not run when the family lacks the two derivatives that it needs. With outer_criterion = NULL, every smooth hyperparameter stays where its term left it and the coefficients of all parameters are fitted at the joint mode, which gives the maximum-likelihood estimate of a dispersion on an ordinary model.

Verbosity

Three levels name the loops: 1 shows the outer search and the alternation, 2 adds the inner method's own iterations, and 3 adds the optimizers' traces. A named logical vector sets the four switches outer, blocks, inner and optimizer independently, and a switch that is left out is off. For example verbose = c(outer = TRUE, blocks = FALSE) shows the hyperparameters moving while a chatty inner optimizer stays silent.

See also

summary.StatmodFit() and predict.StatmodFit() for what to do with the result, statmod_spec() to build the model without fitting it, iwls() for the inner method, reml() and bic() for the criteria, rstatmod() to simulate from a model.

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(200, -2, 2))
dd$y <- 1 + 2 * dd$x + rnorm(200, sd = exp(0.3 * dd$x))

# An ordinary regression: the scale receives an intercept that the
# formula does not specify.
fit <- statmod(y ~ x, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd)
coef(fit)
#> $mu
#> (Intercept)           x 
#>   0.9956298   2.0078791 
#> 
#> $sigma
#> (Intercept) 
#>  0.07592502 
#> 

# The scale is modeled too, which is the purpose of the framework. The data
# were drawn with log sigma = 0.3 x, and the interval covers it.
both <- statmod(y ~ x | sigma ~ x, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd)
coef(both)$sigma
#>  (Intercept)            x 
#> -0.003093138  0.233104770 
confint(both)["sigma:x", c("estimate", "lower", "upper")]
#>          estimate     lower     upper
#> sigma:x 0.2331048 0.1427447 0.3234648

# It is the better model on this data.
c(one = AIC(fit), both = AIC(both))
#>      one     both 
#> 601.9454 578.9246
